Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn Nearly one in three Romanian children aged 9 to 16 has asked their parents to remove content posted about them online, according to EU Kids Online data highlighted in 2026 by Horizon Magazine, the European Commission’s research and innovation publication. Romania recorded the highest percentage in the comparison, at 29%, while Lithuania ranked at the opposite end, with only 3% of children reporting that they had asked their parents to remove such content. In most of the countries surveyed, up to one-third of children said their parents had posted something about them without first asking for their permission. These findings offer a different perspective on digital safety. Research suggests that a child’s first breach of digital privacy may occur within the family itself, when parents begin shaping their child’s online identity before the child is able to decide what they want to make public. The scale of the phenomenon is further highlighted by a 2026 study involving 470 parents who share content about their children online. On average, more than seven of their 20 most recent posts featured at least one of their children. For adults, photos and videos can be a way to preserve memories, share important moments, or stay connected with family and friends. For children, however, the same post can mean losing control over their own image, having a private moment exposed, or acquiring a digital identity they did not choose. As such, sharing content featuring children was associated both with a greater sense of closeness reported by parents and with increased parent–child conflict, particularly when children appeared in content posted on TikTok or YouTube. Isabelle Filliozat, one of Europe’s leading authorities on positive parenting, emotional development and trauma-informed approaches, highlighted respect for children, attention to their needs and recognition of the boundaries they express in relation to the findings. According to her, parents should not treat their child’s image as content they alone have the right to control. Asking for permission before posting, explaining where the photo will appear, respecting the child’s refusal, and removing the content if the child no longer feels comfortable are all ways for adults to show that the child’s voice and boundaries matter. In this context, digital consent becomes a tangible expression of respect within the parent–child relationship, as well as one of the first lessons through which children learn that they have the right to protect their image and privacy. Isabelle Filliozat will make her first appearance in Romania at ParentED Fest, taking place on October 17-18, 2026, at the Aula Magna of the National University of Science and Technology POLITEHNICA Bucharest. Photograph: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Anthropic, the company that developed AI chatbot Claude, says a small team of likely freelance developers in Russia used Claude to develop software for ‘kamikaze’ attack drones. Photograph: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Russia Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Russian developers used AI to build ‘kamikaze’ attack drone software, Anthropic says Anthropic also found that hackers used AI in attacks against targets in Ukrainian government, military and diplomatic sectors. What we know on day 1,662 Guardian staff and agencies Fri 11 Sep 2026 22.12 EDT Last modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 22.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A small team of likely freelance developers in Russia used AI chatbot Claude to develop software for an autonomous swarm of first-person-view “kamikaze” attack drones , including terminal guidance, target selection and coordination between multiple aircraft, according to Anthropic, the company that developed Claude. In a 154-page report describing how bad actors used its Claude AI system for state-sponsored surveillance and propaganda operations, Anthropic said the drone swarm was programmed to pick its own targets and crash into them to detonate, without a human making the final call. In their programming, the freelance team repeatedly picked a location in Ukraine’s Donetsk region as their target and used VPNs to circumvent Anthropic’s geographic blocks. Small drones have become a ‌central weapon in the war in Ukraine. Anthropic ‌also found that cybercriminals and state-backed hackers are increasingly using AI to orchestrate and execute large portions of cyber-attacks , including in attacks targeting officials in Ukraine. One hacking group allegedly ran phishing, hotel wifi hijacking and ​WhatsApp-takeover operations against targets in the Ukrainian government, military and diplomatic sectors, using AI at nearly every stage, Anthropic said. The group’s tradecraft was consistent with Russia-based threat actor Midnight Blizzard, which the US government has previously linked to Russia’s SVR foreign intelligence service, Reuters reported. The Russian embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The group allegedly used AI to build a system that automatically detected when its malware was flagged by security defences and rewrote the code until it evaded detection. The Anthropic report comes as petrol stations in Kyiv have been hit by jet-powered drones in a wave of targeted Russian attacks as the bombardment of Ukraine’s capital enters a new phase of intensity. At least two people were killed and 12 injured in strikes on two petrol stations on Friday morning, according to the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko. The rush-hour strikes follow a similar attack on a petrol station on Thursday. All three strikes targeted petrol stations operated by Ukrnafta, a state-owned oil and natural gas extraction company. A list of 18 petrol stations in Kyiv expected to be hit by Russian drones started circulating on Telegram on Wednesday. The three struck so far were on the list. Russia targets Kyiv petrol stations for first time with jet-powered drones Read more Russian president Vladimir Putin has blamed the west for the conflict in Ukraine because of what he said was its constant pressure on Moscow and its attempts to “drag” Ukraine into the Nato alliance. Speaking to reporters before the BRICS summit in India, Putin said “everything happening in Europe right now is basically ‌the result of system errors by … the western globalists in politics, security, and economics”. After a Russia-friendly president was forced to flee Ukraine in 2014, he said the West “immediately set the goal of dragging Ukraine into Nato. And this ‌ultimately turned out to be the main reason for today’s tragic events in Ukraine”. He said people in Europe understood what was going on, which explained why they were voting for far-right parties such as the AfD in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt. A Russian official will attend a G20 energy meeting in Houston next week, a White House official said on Friday. Last month, the US welcomed ⁠Russian finance minister Anton Siluanov to a meeting of G20 countries in North Carolina, upsetting European officials because it was the first time Russia’s finance ⁠minister had attended the forum in person since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. The meeting comes as European Union efforts to become independent from Russian oil and gas are faltering, as it heads into winter with low gas stocks, its auditors said this month. The US House of Representatives is expected to take up a tough Russian sanctions package next week , although prospects of passage are uncertain despite the bill receiving overwhelming support in the Senate. The bill is designed to add pressure on Putin to negotiate an end to Russia’s war with Ukraine. However, several top Democratic lawmakers are worried the measure dramatically expands president Donald Trump’s tariff authority, and he would use that new power to go after US allies. Three people were killed in Russian ⁠strikes in southeastern Ukraine’s Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia ⁠regions and in Kharkiv in the ​northeast , according to the governors of those regions. Russia has for two weeks been carrying out almost constant attacks with faster jet-powered drones that have killed a number of ⁠Kyiv residents and disrupted daily life in Ukraine’s capital. Ukraine also carried out drone attacks on Russia, killing two people in the Tula region overnight and one on Friday in the Kursk region, local officials said. https://www.politico.eu/article/donald-t.text: U.S. President Donald Trump has signed a deal on the future of Greenland, ending months of transatlantic tensions over his demand to take over the North Atlantic territory. Trump told the United Nations General Assembly in New York that the agreement gives the U.S. “permanent control over security and all other needs.” He said: “We will have the complete ability to do what is necessary to defend the American continent and also Europe and other places.” No U.S. adversary will be permitted to establish a military presence in Greenland or make sensitive investments without American written approval, he said. Advertisement Advertisement Trump promised to build two “very major military bases” on the territory, adding that he’s “formed a bond” with the people of “beautiful” Denmark and the Greenlanders during the negotiations. According to the agreement released by the Danish government, the two new American bases will be located in Narsarsuaq, in southern Greenland at the site of the former American Bluie West One base which closed in the 1950s. The other will be located in Mestersvig, eastern Greenland, currently home to Denmark's Sirius Dog Sled Patrol unit, which will be refurbished. The U.S. military will also have “free access” to air, land and sea routes on the island between the two bases. Greenland is already home to the U.S. Pituffik Space Base, where about 150 American troops are stationed to operate a ballistic missile monitoring site to protect North America from long-range missile attack. “I know it’s going to be a long-term, fantastic relationship,” Trump said at the signing ceremony later, alongside the prime ministers of Denmark, Mette Frederiksen, and Greenland, Jens-Frederik Nielsen. Frederiksen thanked Trump for the deal, labeling it a good one for the U.S., Denmark, and Greenland that would keep enemies and adversaries at bay. The agreement amends and builds on the previous 1951 agreement between the governments of Denmark and the U.S., which gave the U.S. wide latitude to build new military installations and move about the island. It does not cancel or entirely replace the 1951 deal. Advertisement Advertisement New elements make some pointed revisions, however, stipulating that no non-NATO nation can open a base on the island or mine for critical minerals or rare earths without the agreement of the three signatories. Trump has often spoken about Chinese and Russian military activities around Greenland, claiming earlier this year that, "if you take a look outside of Greenland right now, there are Russian destroyers. There are Chinese destroyers … there are Russian submarines all over the place. We're not going to have Russia or China occupy Greenland, and that's what they're going to do if we don't." NATO officials have quietly pushed back against those claims, with one diplomat saying “we’re not seeing any Chinese activity” around Greenland, while Russian movements in the High North haven’t changed significantly and there’s little, if any, Russian presence near Greenland. In a nod to the new prevalence of aerial and naval drones, the agreement also gives the power to Denmark and Greenland to control where — and if — new bases for unmanned platforms can be built on the island. “Denmark together with Greenland shall review requests to establish unmanned military installations in Greenland outside of the Defense Areas under accelerated governmental approval procedures,” the agreement states. “Seventy-five years ago, we entered into an agreement about the defense of Greenland,” Frederiksen said. “Today we are signing an even bigger and better agreement — a deal that can last forever.” Nielsen, Greenland’s premier, said the territory had been supporting U.S. security since World War II. “We are, have been and will remain a steadfast friend of the United States and a part of the Western alliance. Your security is our security, and our security is your security,” he said. Advertisement Advertisement At the start of the year, Trump horrified European allies with his push to annex the sovereign Danish territory and threatened to destabilize NATO, given that Denmark has been a member since the alliance was founded in 1949. In the end, the text of the agreement that Trump signed explicitly reaffirmed Danish sovereignty and the right of Greenlanders to self-determination. Denmark’s European allies welcomed the resolution. European Council President António Costa congratulated Frederiksen and Nielsen but did not mention Trump by name. The deal is “a positive step for transatlantic cooperation and Arctic security, grounded in respect for sovereignty, territorial integrity and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination,” Costa said. “The EU stands ready to continue working closely with Greenland, Denmark and our transatlantic partners for a peaceful, secure and prosperous Arctic.” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz also welcomed the deal. “It is good news that the negotiations of recent months have led to a mutually acceptable solution in line with international law,” he said. The head of state held talks with his Czech counterpart, Prime Minister Andrej Babiš, and the speakers of both chambers of Parliament, alongside a meeting with members of the local Romanian community. According to the Presidential Administration, talks focused on bilateral, European and allied cooperation, with a strong emphasis on European security in the face of threats stemming from Russia’s war against Ukraine. The agenda also covered broader European policy and the expansion of economic ties and investments, including in the defense sector. Cabinet confirmation hearings Meanwhile, parliamentary committees in Bucharest concluded hearings for the cabinet nominees put forward by designated Prime Minister Siegfried Mureșan. Ten candidates faced questioning from lawmakers following Monday’s sessions where only two of the six proposed ministers won committee approval. A decisive floor vote on the government program and cabinet lineup is scheduled for Wednesday in a joint session of Parliament. While PSD and AUR have announced they will vote against the new government, Mureșan, backed by PNL, USR, and UDMR, has vowed to press ahead, saying he will not resign and warning that a defeat risks dragging out a political deadlock that has persisted since May. Passing the legislature requires a minimum of 233 votes. President Nicușor Dan urged an end to the current political standoff, stressing that snap elections are no solution, but would only prolong instability and erode trust among both Romanian citizens and the financial markets. Fraud investigation involving C ălin Georgescu The Bucharest Court of Appeal ruled in favor of prosecutors on Tuesday, ordering that former presidential candidate Călin Georgescu, frequently labeled pro-Russian, be placed under 30-day pre-trial arrest in a case involving fraud and organized crime membership. The same measure was issued for businessman Ionel Rusen, accused of helping raise funds for Georgescu’s 2024 presidential bid. The ruling is final. According to judicial sources cited by media outlets, anti-mafia investigators requested legal assistance from Latvia, Italy, the UK and Switzerland. Estimated damages total €1.1 million, split between alleged investments in precious metals and campaign financing. PwC consumer financial survey On the economic front, only 26% of Romanian consumers describe their financial situation as comfortable, meaning they can clear all monthly bills with money left over for savings and other expenses. That is down 2.5% from last year, according to the global PwC Voice of the Consumer 2026 study. The figure sits well below the Central and Eastern European average of roughly one-third, and significantly trailing the global average of 48%. At the same time, 10.8% of Romanians report that their families struggle to pay monthly bills, up from about 7% in 2025. Data was gathered between February and March 2026 across 27 countries, surveying over 21,000 respondents globally, including 707 in Romania. OECD education report on Romania Finally, education figures show that 23% of young Romanians aged 18 to 24 were neither employed nor in education or training last year, according to the OECD report Education at a Glance 2026 . That rate exceeds the 14% average across member states of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development. The report also notes that 19% of Romanians aged 25 to 64 hold a university degree, compared to an OECD average of 43%. On the bright side, roughly 30% of Romanian higher-education graduates specialize in science, technology, engineering or mathematics (STEM), outpacing the 23% OECD average. However, the study flags that public spending on education remains low, accounting for roughly 6.4% of total public expenditure in 2023, compared to an OECD average of 9.8%. https://english.radio.cz/czech-president.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК Czech President Pavel to meet German Chancellor Merz in Berlin next week Facebook Twitter Czech President Petr Pavel will meet German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin on Wednesday, October 21. Their working meeting will focus, among other things, on foreign and security policy. Pavel will also attend the Berlin Global Dialogue conference, which explores the links between politics, business and geopolitics. He is due to speak on October 22 in a panel discussion on European security and take part in a roundtable organised by the German Council on Foreign Relations. Pavel last visited Berlin in July last year, when he met German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier. After the talks, he said they had confirmed the exceptionally close relations between the two countries.
